THE ACT ITSELF TOOK ONE CALL AND TWO MINUTES; THE GRADE TOOK TWENTY-TWO HOURS, and the twenty-two hours are the part worth keeping. Three readings looked like branch A and none was: a CloudTrail AccessDenied sweep that returned 0 from a plane whose event selectors do not cover this bucket at all; 22 post-delete stages of a chain that started 25 minutes BEFORE the delete; and a union of two partial executions covering 25 of 29 stage keys. The issuer declined the second with a better reason than my own argument against it -- the 7 stages that ran pre-delete are precisely the Schwab-adjacent ones, so I had counted the most stages and the least relevant ones -- and I declined the third myself rather than offer a weaker version of a ruling already made. What finally graded it was a single chain, S_00 23:03:07Z to D_00f 01:12:07Z, every one of its 29 stage keys newer than its own first stage. THE INSTRUMENT LESSON I WOULD CARRY: the checkpoint keys are per-DATE and overwritten per run, so 'the terminal marker exists' is worthless and only 'the terminal marker is newer than THIS run's first stage' is evidence. At any point in those 22 hours a presence check on D_00f would have returned a predecessor's success. The second lesson is smaller and cost me five hours of wrong expectation: I kept predicting a ~04:00Z start when the start hour had already moved twice in the observed window, and the chain that graded this began at 23:03Z. Read the first S_00; do not predict it.
